explanation: Shellac discs spun at about 78 revolutions per minute, so a side held only a few minutes of music. The slower vinyl LP, launched in 1948, held more than 20 minutes a side.

claims.text: A vinyl LP plays at 33 and a third revolutions per minute.
Shellac records spun at about 78 revolutions per minute.
A side of a 78 rpm shellac disc held only a few minutes of music.
The vinyl LP was launched in 1948 and held more than 20 minutes of music per side.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: clean under content:check for writer w-pmusic01w. Claims: every checkable statement in the stem, options and explanation is listed, with risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a fact is beyond everyday knowledge. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers these music facts (the manifest holds geographic, scientific, Nobel, Olympic and art-collection data), so each high-risk claim needs web evidence from the checkers. I used no WebSearch. Rival test: argued for the LP as the newer, 'better' format, which a casual player may take for faster; its 33 and a third rpm is less than half the speed of a 78, so the key stands. 'Old shellac disc' covers early discs, whose speeds varied before 78 became the standard. Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: records and their speeds are the same worldwide. Style: Oxford spelling, straight quotes, no en or em dashes, explanation within 35 words. Myths: screened against myths.json, no hit. Mystery: not applicable to a practice item. Encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: values.a stores 33.33 for 33 and a third; the ratio is far beyond the 1.1 guard.
